notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: conticuere is the first word of Book 2, so the silence of Dido's whole court is the first thing we hear. The reader feels the hush as everyone waits for Aeneas to speak.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: omnes comes straight after the verb and ends its phrase, stressing that every single person is spellbound. It shows how eager the whole hall is to hear the story.

notes.label: Epithet
notes.body: pater presents Aeneas as a father to his people, which shows responsibility as well as respect. He speaks as the leader who must look after the Trojans.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: toro and alto are split, with Aeneas' name and the start of his speech in between. Ending the line on "high" gives him a dignified place as he begins.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: usually used of something monstrous or supernatural

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: infandum opens the line and dolorem closes it, so the grief stretches across the whole line. The separation makes the pain feel vast and heavy.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: how - indirect question introduced by renovare

notes.label: Note
notes.body: a rare word introduced to poetry by Virgil

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: The verb and its subject spill over into line 5, so the destruction of Troy lands with force at the start of the line. The reader feels the shock of the city's fall.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: name for the Greeks used most by Virgil and least by Homer.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: miserrima stresses how wretched the things Aeneas saw were. It makes the reader expect a deeply tragic story.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: The relative pronoun appears twice in different cases (quae, quorum). Aeneas was both a witness and a sufferer, which makes his account personal.

notes.label: Perfect tense
notes.body: fui is short and comes at the end of its sentence. It reminds the reader that Aeneas played a large part in these events, and that Troy now belongs to the past.

notes.label: Variatio
notes.body: Virgil varies his words for "or", using -ve and then aut, which keeps the list of enemies flowing. It makes the list sound natural rather than mechanical.

notes.label: Epithet
notes.body: durus describes Ulysses as hard and pitiless. Even the cruellest of the Greeks, Aeneas suggests, would weep at this story.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three sets of enemies are listed, building up to Ulysses, the most hated. The list stresses that even Troy's fiercest enemies would weep.

notes.label: Delay
notes.body: a lacrimis is held back to the start of line 8, after a long question. The delay makes "tears" land with emotional weight.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: The verb spills over into line 9, so night seems to fall suddenly. It reminds the reader that time is passing and that the story is a long one.

notes.label: Assonance
notes.body: The repeated -ent- sounds in suadentque cadentia create a soft, lulling rhythm. It suits the idea of the stars persuading people to sleep.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated s sounds in sidera somnos are soft and drowsy. The sound helps the reader feel the lateness of the hour.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Understand tibi est

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: casus and nostros are separated by cognoscere, so "our" closes the line. It stresses that these disasters happened to Aeneas' own people.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: supremum and laborem are separated by audire, so "Troy's final suffering" frames the act of hearing. It stresses that this is the end of Troy.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated m sounds slow the line down. They suggest Aeneas' reluctance and pain as he forces himself to remember.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: incipiam is held over to the start of a new line and followed by a full stop. The short, decisive word marks the moment Aeneas makes himself start.

notes.label: Chiasmus
notes.trans: broken by war and thwarted by the fates
notes.body: The words form an ABBA pattern: participle, noun, noun, participle. The balanced phrase sums up how the Greeks were held back by both war and fate.

notes.label: The storyteller
notes.body: Aeneas is telling the story of Troy's fall to Dido and her court at a banquet in Carthage, at the end of Book 1. Books 2 and 3 are his story.

notes.label: The queen
notes.body: Dido, queen of Carthage, who has asked Aeneas to tell how Troy fell.

notes.label: Myrmidons and Dolopes
notes.trans: of the Myrmidons or the Dolopes
notes.body: Greek peoples who fought at Troy: the Myrmidons were Achilles' own men, and the Dolopes followed his son Neoptolemus.

notes.label: Ulysses
notes.body: The Latin name of Odysseus, the cunning Greek hero, whom the Trojans saw as the most ruthless of their enemies. The wooden horse was his idea.

questions: Why do you think Book 2 begins with everyone falling silent?
Aeneas calls his story infandum ("unspeakable") and says his mind shudders to remember it. What does this make the reader expect?
How does Aeneas suggest that even Troy's enemies would be moved by his story?

context.h: Where this comes in the Aeneid
context.body:
At the end of Book 1, Aeneas and his Trojans, shipwrecked on the coast of Africa, have been welcomed by Dido, queen of the new city of Carthage. At a banquet in his honour she asks him to tell the story of the fall of Troy and of his wanderings since. Books 2 and 3 are that story, told by Aeneas himself.

Book 2 is the night Troy fell: the wooden horse, the warning of Laocoön, the lies of Sinon, and the destruction of the city. Because Aeneas is the narrator, we see everything through the eyes of a Trojan who lived through it, and his grief colours every line.
